discoveryHistory: Described by Zhang and Yang in 1995.
interestingFacts: ["One of the last large prosauropods.", "Complete skeleton with skull exhibited in Kunming.", "Quadrupedal browser."]

name: Yunnanosaurus huangi
discoveryHistory: Named by C.C. Young in 1942.
interestingFacts: ["Chisel-like self-sharpening teeth.", "Advanced prosauropod.", "Over 20 complete skeletons recovered."]

name: Bienosaurus lufengensis
discoveryHistory: Described by Dong Zhiming in 2001.
interestingFacts: ["Basal armored thyreophoran.", "Rows of bony osteoderms on back.", "Early Jurassic Asian armored dinosaur."]

name: Lukousaurus yini
discoveryHistory: Named by C.C. Young in 1948.
interestingFacts: ["Small predatory archosaur with horn-like nasal crests.", "Basal theropod or crocodylomorph.", "Lufeng predator."]

name: Eshanosaurus deguchiianus
discoveryHistory: Described by Xu Xing et al. in 2001.
interestingFacts: ["Oldest putative therizinosaurid known.", "Left dentary jaw bone with specialized herbivorous teeth.", "Extends coelurosaur lineage into Early Jurassic."]

name: Sinosaurus triassicus
discoveryHistory: Named by C.C. Young in 1940.
interestingFacts: ["Apex predator of Early Jurassic China.", "Pair of double crests on top of head like Dilophosaurus.", "Deep strong jaws."]

name: Isisaurus colberti
discoveryHistory: Described by Sohan Lal Jain and Saswati Bandyopadhyay in 1997.
interestingFacts: ["Short vertical neck with robust forelimbs.", "Discovered in Dongargaon, Maharashtra.", "Fossilized dung (coprolites) contained angiosperm leaves."]

name: Indochelys spatulata
discoveryHistory: Described by Datta et al. in 2000 from Kota limestone beds, Telangana.
interestingFacts: ["Early aquatic turtle.", "Thick spatulate shell.", "Endemic to Early Jurassic India."]

name: Dandakosaurus indicus
discoveryHistory: Described by Yadagiri in 1982 from Pranhita-Godavari Valley.
interestingFacts: ["Apex theropod predator of Kota Formation.", "Large ceratosaurian relative.", "Named after historic Dandakaranya forest."]

name: Treposuchus indicus
discoveryHistory: Described by Yadagiri in 1988.
interestingFacts: ["Early teleosaurid aquatic crocodile.", "Elongated snout filled with needle teeth.", "Freshwater lagoon inhabitant."]

name: Sivapithecus sivalensis
discoveryHistory: First discovered by Falconer and Cautley in 1836 in Siwalik Hills, India.
interestingFacts: ["Direct ancestor of modern orangutans (Pongo).", "Concave facial profile and tall oval eye sockets.", "Thick tooth enamel for crushing tough seeds."]

name: Gigantopithecus bilaspurensis
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1968 near Bilaspur, Himachal Pradesh, India.
interestingFacts: ["Largest primate to ever live.", "Massive lower jaw with huge grinding molars.", "Forest floor browser."]

name: Bramatherium megacephalum
discoveryHistory: Described by Hugh Falconer in 1845 from Siwalik strata.
interestingFacts: ["Massive extinct giraffid.", "Five crown ossicones forming a helmet crest.", "Stocky neck and body frame."]

name: Hexaprotodon sivalensis
discoveryHistory: Described by Falconer and Cautley in 1836.
interestingFacts: ["Primitive hippopotamus with 6 incisors instead of 4.", "Semiaquatic river basin dweller.", "Widespread across Neogene India."]

name: Archidiskodon planifrons
discoveryHistory: Described by Falconer and Cautley in 1845.
interestingFacts: ["Early mammoth ancestor.", "Curved tusks up to 3 meters.", "Transition to grassland grazing."]

name: Bahariasaurus ingens
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Ernst Stromer in 1912; original fossils destroyed in WWII bombing of Munich in 1944.
interestingFacts: ["Rivaled Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus in length.", "Large slender theropod.", "Tragically lost holotype specimen."]

name: Aegyptosaurus baharijensis
discoveryHistory: Named by Ernst Stromer in 1932.
interestingFacts: ["Primitive African titanosaur.", "Found in coastal mangrove swamp deposits.", "Fossils also destroyed in Munich 1944 bombing."]

name: Stromerichthys lacustris
discoveryHistory: Named by Weiler in 1935 in honor of Ernst Stromer.
interestingFacts: ["Giant bichir ray-finned fish.", "Heavy ganoid scales.", "Inhabited Bahariya freshwater estuaries."]

name: Abrictosaurus consors
discoveryHistory: Described by Richard Thulborn in 1974.
interestingFacts: ["Early heterodontosaurid without prominent upper tusks.", "Slender bipedal runner.", "Found in Upper Elliot Formation."]

name: Santanadactylus brasilensis
discoveryHistory: Described by de Buisonjé in 1980.
interestingFacts: ["Early anhanguerid pterosaur.", "Preserved in Araripe calcareous nodules.", "Slender wing bones."]

name: Mamenchisaurus constructus
discoveryHistory: Described by C.C. Young in 1954 from Sichuan.
interestingFacts: ["Extremely long neck making up half of body length.", "19 cervical neck vertebrae.", "Shaximiao apex browser."]

name: Halszkaraptor escuilliei
discoveryHistory: Described by Andrea Cau et al. in 2017.
interestingFacts: ["Amphibious swan-necked dromaeosaurid.", "Paddle-like forelimbs for swimming.", "Synchrotron micro-tomography discovery."]

name: Shuvuuia deserti
discoveryHistory: Described by Chiappe et al. in 1998 from Ukhaa Tolgod.
interestingFacts: ["Extreme low-frequency night hearing adaptations.", "Single stout claw on short arms for digging anthills.", "Keratinous beta-feather proteins preserved."]

name: Talarurus plicatospineus
discoveryHistory: Named by Maleev in 1952.
interestingFacts: ["Heavy bony tail club.", "Interlocking armored osteoderms.", "Found in Nemegt river beds."]

name: Homalocephale calathocercos
discoveryHistory: Described by Maryanska and Osmolska in 1974.
interestingFacts: ["Flat-topped pachycephalosaur skull.", "Broad pelvis for live birth or large digestive tract.", "Found in Nemegt Basin."]

name: Prenocephale prenes
discoveryHistory: Described by Maryanska and Osmolska in 1974.
interestingFacts: ["Thick domed skull roof surrounded by bony spikes.", "High visual capabilities.", "Agile bipedal runner."]

name: Jainosaurus septentrionalis
discoveryHistory: Named by Hunt et al. in 1994 in honor of Sohan Lal Jain.
interestingFacts: ["Large titanosaur from Jabalpur.", "Distinct braincase structure.", "Coexisted with Rajasaurus."]

name: Lametasaurus indicus
discoveryHistory: Described by Charles Matley in 1923 from Bara Simla, Jabalpur.
interestingFacts: ["Armor osteoderms found associated with theropod bones.", "Historic Indian abelisaurid taxon.", "Lameta Formation discovery."]

name: Kotaichthys kartikeyai
discoveryHistory: Described by Yabumoto and Gururaja in 2007.
interestingFacts: ["Freshwater ray-finned fish.", "Found in Kota limestone beds of Telangana.", "Heavy ganoid scales."]

name: Indobatrachus pusillus
discoveryHistory: First described by Owen in 1847.
interestingFacts: ["Early fossil frog specimen.", "Preserved complete skeleton in lake shale.", "Kota formation lake fauna."]

name: Paralititan stromeri
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 2001 by Joshua Smith et al. in Bahariya Oasis.
interestingFacts: ["Colossal 42-ton titanosaur.", "Found in coastal mangrove tidal flat deposits.", "1.69m humerus bone."]

name: Blikanasaurus cromptoni
discoveryHistory: Described by Galton and van Heerden in 1985.
interestingFacts: ["Heavy stocky quadrupedal sauropodomorph lower limb.", "Found in Lower Elliot Formation.", "Early stage of sauropod gigantism."]

name: Spinosaurus maroccanus
discoveryHistory: Described by Dale Russell in 1996 from Kem Kem Beds.
interestingFacts: ["Moroccan spinosaur species based on cervical vertebrae length.", "Specialized fish-eating snout.", "Inhabited Kem Kem river deltas."]

name: Yangchuanosaurus shangyouensis
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1977 during Yongchuan dam construction in Sichuan.
interestingFacts: ["Apex carnosaur predator of Late Jurassic China.", "Rugged facial crests on top of nose.", "Deep powerful jaws."]

name: Opisthocoelicaudia skarzynskii
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1965 by Polish-Mongolian expedition in Nemegt Basin.
interestingFacts: ["Opposite cavity tail vertebrae for rigid tripod stance.", "Lacked clawed fingers on forelimbs.", "Complete skeleton minus skull."]

name: Compsosuchus solus
discoveryHistory: Described by von Huene and Matley in 1933 from Bara Simla, Jabalpur.
interestingFacts: ["Small slender noasaurid theropod.", "Distinct hollow neck vertebrae.", "Cretaceous Indian predator."]

name: Eocarcharia dinops
discoveryHistory: Described by Paul Sereno and Stephen Brusatte in 2008.
interestingFacts: ["Heavy brow ridge over eye socket.", "Bladelike serrated teeth for flesh cutting.", "Early carcharodontosaurid."]

name: Chungkingosaurus jiangbeiensis
discoveryHistory: Described by Dong Zhiming et al. in 1983 from Chongqing.
interestingFacts: ["Smallest known stegosaurid from Shaximiao Formation.", "Multiple pairs of thagomizer tail spikes.", "Thick dorsal armor plates."]

name: Squalicorax falcatus
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America, Europe, Africa","region":"Western Interior Seaway","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Niobrara Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Louis Agassiz in 1843 from teeth found in Cretaceous marine strata.
• Fossilized teeth are extremely common across North American and European Cretaceous marine deposits.
• In 2010, a specimen was discovered with fossilized bones of a mosasaur inside its stomach region.
sizeNotes: Average length between 2 to 5 meters, with serrated teeth specialized for cutting.
interestingFacts: ["Known as the 'Crow Shark' due to its ubiquitous presence as a scavenger in Cretaceous seas.","Fossilized Squalicorax teeth have been found embedded in the bones of terrestrial dinosaurs, proving it scavenged on carcasses washed out to sea.","Possessed distinctive serrated, crescent-shaped teeth perfect for slicing through tough flesh and bone."]

name: Zalmoxes robustus
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Baron Franz Nopcsa in 1900 under the genus Mochlodon.
• Reclassified as the distinct genus Zalmoxes by Weishampel et al. in 2003.
• Nopcsa used Zalmoxes fossils to formulate his pioneering theory of insular dwarfism in dinosaurs.
sizeNotes: Classic example of insular dwarfism; significantly smaller than mainland iguanodontians.
interestingFacts: ["Lived on Hațeg Island, an isolated landmass in Late Cretaceous Europe, leading to insular dwarfism.","Possessed a surprisingly robust, heavy skull compared to its small overall body size.","Served as a primary herbivorous prey species for the giant azhdarchid pterosaur Hatzegopteryx."]

name: Geosaurus giganteus
discoveryHistory:
• Formally named by Georges Cuvier in 1824 from fossils discovered in Bavaria, Germany.
• Exceptionally preserved Solnhofen limestone fossils revealed soft-tissue impressions of tail flukes.
• Redescribed extensively in 2009 by Young & Andrade, clarifying its hyper-carnivorous adaptations.
sizeNotes: Streamlined marine crocodilian with paddle-like limbs and a hypocercal tail fluke.
interestingFacts: ["Completely lost heavy osteoderm armor to maximize aquatic agility and swimming speed.","Transformed its legs into hydrofoil paddles and developed a fish-like hypocercal tail fin.","Equipped with serrated, ziphodont teeth optimized for tearing prey rather than crushing shells."]

name: Metriorhynchus geoffroyii
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe","region":"English Channel Basin","country":"United Kingdom, France","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• Named by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1830.
• Abundant specimens recovered from the Jurassic Oxford Clay of Peterborough, England.
• Histological studies confirm it spent its entire life in open marine environments.
sizeNotes: Fully aquatic thalattosuchian crocodilian measuring approximately 3 meters.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed large salt glands positioned above its eyes to excrete excess ocean salt.","Gave live birth at sea (viviparity) as its limbs could no longer support walking on land.","Had smooth skin without armor scales, reducing drag in the water."]

name: Megaraptor namunhuaiquii
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1998 by Fernando Novas in Neuquén Province, Argentina.
• Initially mistaken for a giant dromaeosaurid due to an enormous claw assumed to belong to the foot.
• 2004 discovery of complete forelimbs revealed the massive sickle claw actually belonged to the hand (Digit I).
sizeNotes: Large megaraptoran theropod characterized by immense 35-centimeter hand claws.
interestingFacts: ["Its famous 35 cm sickle claw was originally misidentified as a giant foot claw like Velociraptor's.","Head of the enigmatic Megaraptora clade, which dominated South American ecosystems after carcharodontosaurids declined.","Possessed highly pneumatic (air-filled) bones, making it agile for an 8-meter long predator."]

name: Maip macrothorax
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2019 by Alexis Aranciaga Rolando and team in Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
• Formally described in Scientific Reports in April 2022.
• Preserved vertebrae, ribs, coracoid, gastralia, and partial pelvis.
sizeNotes: Largest known megaraptoran theropod, reaching up to 10 meters long and 5 tonnes.
interestingFacts: ["Named 'Maip' after an evil mythological spirit of the Aonikenk (Tehuelche) people representing cold death.","The largest megaraptoran ever discovered, outsizing Megaraptor and Australovenator.","Had an unusually wide, heavy thoracic cavity ('macrothorax') housing large lung systems for high metabolism."]

name: Lythronax argestes
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2009 in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, Utah.
• Formally described in 2013 by Mark Loewen and colleagues.
• Holotype specimen UMNH VP 20200 includes skull, postcranial elements, and gastralia.
sizeNotes: Estimated at 8 meters in length and 2.5 tonnes; earliest true tyrannosaurid known.
interestingFacts: ["Nickname 'Gore King' comes from its scientific name translating directly to 'King of Gore'.","Possessed broad skull rear and narrow snout, giving it overlapping 3D binocular vision like T. rex 13 million years earlier.","Proved that tyrannosaurid radiation occurred much earlier than previously assumed."]

name: Moros intrepidus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Emery County, Utah, after a decade-long search led by Lindsay Zanno.
• Formally described in Communications Biology in February 2019.
• Represents the earliest diagnostic Cretaceous tyrannosauroid in North America.
sizeNotes: Small, lightweight cursorial tyrannosauroid standing less than a meter high at the hip.
interestingFacts: ["Filled the 70-million-year gap in North American tyrannosaur evolution.","Existed as a small, nimble predator when giant allosauroids (like Siats) were apex predators.","Extremely long leg bones indicate superior running speed and cursorial agility."]

name: Sauroposeidon proteles
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Gulf Coast / Interior Plains","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Antlers Formation, Cloverly Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• Four massive neck vertebrae discovered in Oklahoma in 1994 by prison trainer Bobby Cross.
• Initially stored as petrified wood for five years before paleontologists recognized their true nature.
• Formally described in 2000 by Mathew Wedel, Richard Cifelli, and Kent Sanders.
sizeNotes: Stood up to 18 meters (60 feet) high, making it one of the tallest land animals to ever live.
interestingFacts: ["Its neck reached up to 12 meters (39 feet) in length, accounting for over one-third of its total body length.","Cervical vertebrae were up to 1.4 meters long and filled with honeycombed internal air cells (trabecular bone).","Stood as tall as a 6-story building, allowing it to browse vegetation inaccessible to any other creature."]

name: Psephoderma alpinum
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1858.
• Complete articulated specimens recovered from the Italian Alps (Zorzino Limestone).
• Represents one of the last surviving placodonts before the end-Triassic extinction.
sizeNotes: Turtle-like marine placodont with a flattened, armored body split into two shields.
interestingFacts: ["Superficially resembled a marine turtle but belonged to the extinct placodont order of sauropterygians.","Had two distinct protective carapace shields: one covering the shoulders/chest and a smaller one over the pelvis.","Possessed toothless, narrow beaked jaws lined internally with flat, pavement-like crushing plates."]

name: Vayuraptor agriculturalis
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 during agricultural field excavations in Chaiyaphum Province, Thailand.
• Formally described in 2019 by Adun Samathi and colleagues.
• Named in honor of the Sanskrit wind god Vayu due to its lightweight, fast-running skeletal adaptations.
sizeNotes: Medium-sized basal coelurosaurian theropod estimated at 4.5 meters in length.
interestingFacts: ["Coexisted with another medium-sized theropod, Siamraptor, in Early Cretaceous Thailand.","Ankle bones (astragalus and calcaneum) were fused together, enhancing biomechanical sprinting stability.","Species name 'agriculturalis' honors local farmers who assisted in uncovering the fossil site."]

name: Rhizodus hibberti
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Richard Owen in 1840 from massive tooth specimens found near Edinburgh.
• Fossilized scales up to 30 cm across and 22 cm long tusk-teeth were recovered in Scottish coal fields.
• Biomechanical studies confirm massive pectoral fin musculature for rapid burst acceleration.
sizeNotes: The largest known freshwater lobe-finned fish, reaching up to 7 meters in length.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed enormous 22 cm (9 inch) tusk-like teeth anchored deeply into massive jaws.","Could likely lung onto land or shallow swamp margins to snatch terrestrial amphibians, similar to modern crocodiles.","Its skin was covered in heavy, overlapping cosmoid scales providing armor against rival aquatic predators."]

name: Gillicus arcuatus
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America","region":"Western Interior Seaway","country":"United States","fossilFormation":"Smoky Hill Chalk"}
discoveryHistory:
• First named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1872.
• Famous for the 'Fish-Within-A-Fish' fossil at the Sternberg Museum where a 4.3m Xiphactinus contains an intact 2m Gillicus in its ribcage.
• Abundant in Kansas chalk deposits.
sizeNotes: Slender, 2-meter long ichthyodectid fish with fine, toothless or tiny-toothed jaws.
interestingFacts: ["Best known as the swallowed prey in the famous 14-foot Xiphactinus specimen at Hays, Kansas.","Possessed numerous fine, needle-like gill rakers used to strain small marine organisms from sea water.","Had deeply embedded, thin circular scales that reduced turbulence during swift schooling swims."]

name: Yutyrannus huali
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by local fossil collectors in Liaoning Province, China, and acquired by Xu Xing.
• Formally described in Nature in April 2012 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
• Three nearly complete skeletons of varying ages preserved extensive filamentous plumage.
sizeNotes: Largest known dinosaur with direct, fossilized evidence of feathers.
interestingFacts: ["Holds the record as the largest direct feather-bearing animal in Earth's history (9 meters long, 1.4 tonnes).","Feathers were 20 cm long filamentous proto-feathers providing insulation in Liaoning's chilly 10°C climate.","Possessed a high median crest along its snout used for species display and intra-species communication."]

name: Nanotyrannus lancensis
discoveryHistory:
• Skull discovered in 1942 by Charles W. Gilmore and initially named Gorgosaurus lancensis.
• Renamed Nanotyrannus by Robert Bakker, Michael Williams, and Philip Currie in 1988.
• Long debated whether it is a valid distinct genus or a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex; 2024 studies by Longrich & Saitta reignited support for its validity.
sizeNotes: Slender, long-limbed theropod measuring roughly 5 meters in length and weighing ~900 kg.
interestingFacts: ["Subject of one of the longest and most fiercely contested debates in paleontology history.","Had significantly more teeth (up to 36 in upper jaw) and larger forelimbs than adult T. rex.","Possessed extremely long, slender leg bones adapted for high-speed pursuit running."]

name: Palaeoloxodon antiquus
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe, Asia","region":"Mediterranean & Central Europe","country":"Germany, United Kingdom, Italy, Greece","fossilFormation":"Ebbsfleet Valley deposits"}
discoveryHistory:
• Formally described in 1847 by Hugh Falconer and Proby Cautley.
• Numerous butchered skeletons discovered across Europe alongside Neanderthal flint tools.
• Genomic analysis in 2017 revealed Palaeoloxodon is closely related to modern African forest elephants.
sizeNotes: Stood up to 4.2 meters tall at the shoulder and weighed up to 13-15 metric tonnes.
interestingFacts: ["One of the largest terrestrial mammals to ever walk the Earth, outsizing the Woolly Mammoth.","Possessed long, nearly straight tusks reaching up to 3.8 meters in length.","Coexisted with Neanderthals and early Homo sapiens, who actively hunted these leviathans with wooden spears."]

name: Gryposuchus colombianus
geographicRange: {"continent":"South America","region":"Amazon & Orinoco Basins","country":"Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil","fossilFormation":"La Venta Formation, Urumaco Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Langston in 1965 from fossils collected at La Venta, Colombia.
• Exceptionally complete skulls recovered from Miocene deposits in Venezuela and Peru.
• Represents one of the largest members of the gharial family Gavialidae.
sizeNotes: Giant gharial-like crocodilian reaching estimated lengths of 10 meters.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed an extremely elongated, narrow snout packed with over 80 inter-locking needle teeth.","Inhabited the mega-wetlands of Miocene South America alongside giant caimans like Purussaurus.","The hook-like curvature at the tip of its snout helped hold onto slippery, armor-plated prehistoric catfish."]

name: Plesiosuchus manselii
discoveryHistory:
• Named by Richard Owen in 1884 based on a skull found in Kimmeridge Bay, Dorset.
• Re-analyzed in 2012 by Mark Young and colleagues, establishing Plesiosuchus as the apex predator of Kimmeridgian seas.
sizeNotes: The largest known metriorhynchid marine crocodilian, reaching almost 7 meters.
interestingFacts: ["The largest metriorhynchid crocodilian ever discovered, outgrowing Geosaurus and Metriorhynchus.","Had wide-opening jaws with coarse serrations adapted for severing flesh from large marine vertebrates.","Shared marine habitats with Dakosaurus, dividing ecological niches based on skull mechanics."]

name: Suchodus durobrivensis
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe","region":"Oxford Clay Basin","country":"United Kingdom, France","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Lydekker in 1890 from specimens collected near Peterborough, England.
• Re-erected as a distinct genus separate from Metriorhynchus by Young et al. in 2010.
sizeNotes: Robust metriorhynchid crocodilian measuring 4.5 meters in length.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed significantly shorter, stronger jaws than Metriorhynchus for crushing armored prey.","Equipped with paddle-shaped limbs and a tail fin for pelagic sea life.","Fossilized eye rings (sclerotic rings) show adaptations for deep diving."]

name: Edestus heinrichi
geographicRange: {"continent":"North America, Europe","region":"Illinois Basin","country":"United States, Russia","fossilFormation":"Carbondale Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Joseph Leidy in 1855 from bracketed tooth whorls found in coal mines.
• 2019 jaw mechanics study confirmed vertical slashing jaw action.
sizeNotes: Nicknamed the 'Scissor-toothed Shark'; reached lengths of up to 6 meters.
interestingFacts: ["Did not shed worn teeth; new teeth grew in from the back, pushing old teeth forward into protruding curved brackets.","Jaws operated like a pair of hedge trimmers, thrashing up and down to slash prey.","Belonged to Eugeneodontida, closely related to modern chimaeras rather than true sharks."]

name: Pyroraptor olympius
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1992 following a forest fire at Mount Olympe near Trets, Provence, France.
• Formally described in 2000 by Ronan Allain and Philippe Taquet.
• Remains include distinctive sickle toe claws, teeth, limb bones, and vertebrae.
sizeNotes: Small dromaeosaurid dinosaur measuring 1.6 meters long and standing knee-high.
interestingFacts: ["Named 'Fire Thief' because its fossils were uncovered immediately after a major forest fire.","Possessed a curved 6.5 cm sickle claw on the second toe of each foot for gripping prey.","Fully covered in feathers with wing-like plumage along its forelimbs."]

name: Dracovenator regenti
discoveryHistory:
• Holotype partial skull discovered on Upper Drakensberg farm in Eastern Cape, South Africa.
• Named in 2005 by Adam M. Yates.
• Close relative of the North American Dilophosaurus.
sizeNotes: Dilophosaurid theropod estimated at 5.5 to 6 meters long.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest apex theropod dinosaurs discovered in southern Africa.","Possessed paired bony crests running along the top of its skull.","Targeted abundant early sauropodomorph dinosaurs as primary prey."]

name: Sarcosaurus woodi
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1913 near Barrow-upon-Soar, Leicestershire, by James W. Wood.
• Named by Charles William Andrews in 1921.
• Represents one of the oldest known Jurassic theropods in Europe.
sizeNotes: Basal neotheropod measuring 3.5 meters in length.
interestingFacts: ["One of the earliest true Jurassic theropod dinosaurs discovered in the UK.","Possessed a small nasal horn or crest similar to Ceratosaurus.","Inhabited coastal mudflats alongside early marine reptiles."]

name: Animantarx ramaljonesi
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 using radiological survey equipment by Ramal Jones.
• Formally described by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Donald Burge, and John Bird in 1999.
• Discovered specifically due to radioactive signals emitted by fossilized bones.
sizeNotes: Small nodosaurid ankylosaur measuring approximately 3 meters.
interestingFacts: ["First dinosaur discovered exclusively via radiological radiation detection technology.","Possessed a heavily armored skull with small horn-like projections behind the eyes.","Lacked a tail club, relying instead on shoulder spikes and fused armor plates."]

name: Segnosaurus galbinensis
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1973 in the Gobi Desert by Altangerel Perle.
• Formally described by Perle in 1979.
• Name-giver of the Segnosauria (now Therizinosauria) group.
sizeNotes: Large therizinosaurid measuring 6 meters in length and weighing over 1 tonne.
interestingFacts: ["Bizarre theropod that evolved away from meat-eating to become a strict herbivore.","Possessed a massive pot belly to ferment tough plant vegetation.","Equipped with elongated, curved hand claws used to pull down tree branches."]

name: Bajadasaurus pronuspinax
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2013 in Neuquén Province, Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally described in Scientific Reports in 2019 by Pablo Gallina and colleagues.
• Preserved skull, neck vertebrae, and spectacular elongated neural spines.
sizeNotes: Dicraeosaurid sauropod measuring 9 meters long with dramatic forward-pointing neck spines.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed extremely long, thin neural spines along its neck that curved forward over its head.","The neck spines were likely covered in keratin sheaths, acting as defensive spikes against predators while grazing.","Eyes were positioned high on its skull, allowing it to look out for predators while lowering its snout to eat."]

name: Fukuiraptor kitadaniensis
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 at the Kitadani Quarry in Katsuyama, Fukui Prefecture, Japan.
• Formally described in 2000 by Yoichi Azuma and Philip J. Currie.
• One of the most complete theropod skeletons found in Japan.
sizeNotes: Medium-sized megaraptoran theropod reaching 4.2 meters in length.
interestingFacts: ["Initially thought to be a dromaeosaurid due to a large hand claw, later recognized as a megaraptoran.","The state dinosaur mascot of Fukui Prefecture, Japan.","Possessed large hand claws used to grasp prey."]

name: Fukuisaurus tetoriensis
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1989 alongside Fukuiraptor in Katsuyama, Fukui, Japan.
• Described in 2003 by Yoichi Azuma and Pascal Godefroit.
• Preserved skull and jaw material showing unique kinetic chewing adaptations.
interestingFacts: ["Skull lacked the kinetic flexibility seen in advanced hadrosaurs, chewing with a rigid maxilla.","Coexisted with Fukuiraptor, Fukuititan, and Koshisaurus in Early Cretaceous Japan.","Equipped with a sharp beak for clipping tough vegetation."]

name: Leedsichthys problematicus
geographicRange: {"continent":"Europe, South America","region":"Tethys / Boreal Oceans","country":"United Kingdom, France, Germany, Chile","fossilFormation":"Oxford Clay Formation"}
discoveryHistory:
• First fragments collected in 1886 near Peterborough, England, by fossil collector Alfred Nicholson Leeds.
• Named 'problematicus' by Arthur Smith Woodward because giant fragmented bones were difficult to reconstruct.
• Comprehensive 2013 laser-scan study by Jeff Liston confirmed adult lengths between 16 and 16.5 meters.
sizeNotes: The largest bony fish (Osteichthyes) known to have ever existed, reaching 16.5 meters.
interestingFacts: ["Holds the record as the largest bony fish in Earth's history, rivaling modern baleen whales in ecological role.","Possessed over 40,000 delicate mesh-like gill raker teeth to filter microscopic plankton.","Bite marks on Leedsichthys fins show it was hunted by giant marine predators like Liopleurodon and Metriorhynchus."]

name: Suchomimus tenerensis
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1997 in the Ténéré Desert of Niger by team led by Paul Sereno.
• Formally described in Science in November 1998.
• Skeleton roughly 70% complete including skull, arms, claws, and vertebrae.
sizeNotes: Large spinosaurid theropod measuring 11 meters in length and weighing nearly 4 tonnes.
interestingFacts: ["Possessed a narrow 1.2-meter long crocodile-like skull lined with 100 conical teeth.","Had a massive 30 cm sickle claw on its thumb used to spear fish.","Featured a low neural spine sail reaching up to 60 cm high along its back."]

name: Oxalaia quilombensis
discoveryHistory:
• Premaxilla discovered in 1999 on Cajual Island, Maranhão, Brazil.
• Formally described in 2011 by Alexander Kellner and colleagues.

name: Tropaeognathus mesembrinus

name: Coloborhynchus clavirostris

• Named by Richard Owen in 1874 based on a partial snout found in East Sussex, England.

name: Arctodus simus

name: Varanus priscus
